headline.en: A shanty kept a ship's crew pulling together. Sing it strong, not loud, over a drone: one note held underneath, like a bagpipe's.

detail.en: Drunken Sailor, the first verse
You're the crew
Strong, never pushed

text.en: The first line, at your own pace. Each note waits until you find it.
Listen to two lines, then sing them back.
Now the last two lines. Listen for the bright note in "drunk-en".

measures.en: Your stars are for the notes of the last two lines. You just sang a shanty. That bright note in "drunk-en" is why it sounds old: you'll meet it again in unit 2. Next: hear the wobble vanish.

headline.en: A note a little out of tune beats against the drone, a wobble in the sound. In tune, the wobble goes and the two ring as one.

detail.en: Your note and the drone, as one sound
Like a relaxed sigh, never squeezed
Softer, never held still

text.en: Listen to each with the drone, as often as you like, then choose.

prompt.en: Which one rings with the drone?

why.en: B was a little high: hear the quick wobble in the sound? A rings as one with the drone.

prompt.en: Which one rings with the drone?

why.en: A was a little low. Its wobble was slower, because it was closer.

prompt.en: Which one rings with the drone?

why.en: Closer still, so the beats were slower. B wasn't quite one sound with the drone yet.

prompt.en: Which one rings with the drone?

why.en: The hardest one: a slow pulse, almost gone. In tune, it's gone.

text.en: Find the drone's note and hold it. Listen for the wobble going.
Start a touch low, slide up until the wobble goes, then hold it, plain and easy.

measures.en: Your stars are for how long you held the note on pitch with the drone, and how steadily. Next: telling a story in song.

headline.en: A ballad is a story. Each word gets its own time, the way you'd tell it.

detail.en: Barbara Allen, a ballad hundreds of years old
"Town", "born", "fair"
So every word reaches the listener

text.en: Sing the first line along with the guide, at your own pace.
Listen, then tell the whole line back over the drone.

measures.en: Your stars are for the notes; the rhythm is yours to tell. Listen back: could someone hear every word? Next: the whole verse.

headline.en: The whole first verse, on your own over the drone, every long note plain.

detail.en: Two lines, one story
Halfway, where the line turns
A light wave is fine, never squeezed

text.en: After a bar of the drone, sing the verse.

measures.en: Your stars are for the notes. Listen back: were the long notes plain and steady?

headline.en: You've sung this already. The bright note in "drunk-en" is what makes it sound old: a minor tune with one note higher. That's the Dorian mode.

detail.en: The second note of "drunk-en"
One note higher than plain minor
So you can hear how it colours the tune

text.en: The Dorian scale from the home note up six notes and back. The sixth is the bright one.
After a bar of the drone, sing the last two lines. Make the bright note bright.

measures.en: Your stars are for the notes, the bright one among them. Next: the soft note, its major cousin.

headline.en: Old Joe Clark is a major tune with one note lower: a soft seventh. That's the Mixolydian mode, the sound of many old-time fiddle tunes.

detail.en: Old Joe Clark, a dance tune from the Appalachians
On "a-" of "away", just below the home note
One note lower than a major tune would sing

text.en: The scale from the soft note below the home note up to the fifth, and back.
After a bar of the drone, sing the chorus. Light and bouncy, strong, not loud.

measures.en: Your stars are for the notes, the soft one among them. Next: tell the modes apart by ear.

headline.en: Two short tunes over the same drone, one note apart. Which mode is it?

detail.en: Minor with a raised sixth: Dorian
Major with a lowered seventh: Mixolydian

title.en: Listen as often as you like

detail.en: Only your first answer counts

prompt.en: Which one has the bright note?

why.en: B's sixth was bright: that's Dorian. A's was dark: plain minor.
A had the bright sixth near the top. B's was a step darker.

prompt.en: Which one has the soft note?

why.en: A's seventh was soft, one note lower than major's: that's Mixolydian.
B's seventh was soft. A's leaned right up into the top note: plain major.
Coming down, B touched the bright sixth first. A's sixth was dark.
A stepped down to a soft seventh. B's seventh was the bright one of major.
A was minor-sounding with a bright sixth: Dorian. B was major with a soft seventh: Mixolydian.
B was major with a soft seventh. A sounded minor, with a bright sixth: Dorian.

measures.en: Your stars are for the rounds you got right first time. Next: a whole shanty, on your own.

headline.en: Drunken Sailor again, the whole verse, with no one to echo now. Make the bright note bright and keep the long notes plain.

detail.en: Then it's yours
"morn-ing" steady and easy
A crew sings together, not over each other

text.en: After a bar of the drone, sing the verse.

measures.en: Your stars are for the notes. Listen back, then hear your first try from lesson 1: how far you've come.
